newsitem.title: USA: GPU offers Pennsylvania competition plan.
newsitem.headline: GPU offers Pennsylvania competition plan.

text.p: GPU Energy said Monday it detailed plans filed with the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission to implement competition and customer choice in the electric industry.
As a result of this proposal, the GPU Inc subsidiary said, it projects stranded costs in Pennsylvania of over #1 billion.
The company said it expects to file a request with the commission later this year for permission to issue transition bonds to securitize and pay off an undisclosed portion of its stranded costs.

As part of its announcement, GPU Energy disclosed GPU Generation's current plans anticipate closing Pennsylvania Electric Co's Warren and Seward generating stations by the year 2000 and Metropolitan Edison's Portland and Titus generating stations by the year 2004.

These coal-fired plants, located in the Pennsylvania communities of the same names, have rated capacities or 82 megawatts at Warren, 196 megawatts at Seward, 401 megawatts at Portland and 243 megawatts at Titus.
GPU's two Pennsylvania subsidiaries do business under the GPU Energy trade name.

GPU said the restructuring plans for its two Pennsylvania subsidiaries outline a transition to providing customers with access to a competitive generation market under the provisions of Pennsylvania's competition law.

GPU Energy President Dennis Baldassari, "As an early advocate of competition in Pennsylvania, we are pleased to be 'inventing the future of energy' in terms of how we move forward with customer choice starting January 1, 1999."
Extensive computer modeling was done to simulate the future power market and project electricity prices in the competitive environment.

Based on those prices, GPU Energy's filing estimates its stranded costs -- investments and commitments made to serve customers that may not be recoverable in a competitive environment -- at about $641 million for Met-Ed and about $372 million for Penelec.
In addition, the stranded costs include the two utilities' obligations to purchase power from non-utility generators.

Thus the total stranded costs will not be known until the non-utility generators respond to GPU's reverse auction offer of up to $1 billion to buy out or buy down their contracts, spokesman Gary Plummer said.
Those bids are due today, he said.

The competition law gives utilities the opportunity to fully recover their prudently incurred stranded costs through a Competitive Transition Charge to be paid by all customers utilizing GPU Energy's distribution system.

Baldassari said GPU Energy expects to file a request with the commission later this year for permission to securitize an undisclosed portion of its stranded costs -- that is, issue transition bonds to pay off these costs.
GPU said the commission will review and hold hearings on the restructuring filing.
A decision on the plans is due by early March 1998.

Under the competition law, GPU Energy said, it will "unbundle" its rates. This means separate charges will be shown on the bills of customers for the different aspects of electric service. These include generation, which is the cost of producing electricity; transmission, which is the movement of power over high-voltage lines from the generating site to distribution points; and distribution, which is the local delivery of electricity to homes and businesses.
GPU Energy also said it has rewritten and simplified its tariffs to make them more "user friendly."
Where it was possible, common provisions were established for Met-Ed and Penelec.
